```{r}
 library(tidyverse)
 library(here)
library(plotly)
source(here("R", "other.R"))
plots <- read_rds(here("out","plots.rds"))
lfs_data <- read_rds(here("out", "lfs_data.rds"))
noc_specificity <- read_rds(here("out", "noc_specificity.rds"))
hier <- read_rds(here("out", "hier.rds"))
skills <- read_rds(here("out","skills.rds"))
skills_mat <- skills[["skills_noc_dist"]]
skills_hc  <- hclust(as.dist(skills_mat), method = "average")
skills_ord <- skills_hc$order
skills_mat_ord <- skills_mat[skills_ord, skills_ord]
skills_xlab <- as.character(colnames(skills_mat_ord))
skills_ylab <- as.character(rownames(skills_mat_ord))
dest_plt <- noc_specificity|>
  ggplot(aes(T, specificity, text=noc, fill=gating_quartile)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d()+
  geom_point(shape=21, size=3, stroke=.5) +
  scale_x_log10(labels=scales::comma)+
  labs(fill="Gating Quartile")
```

## Do Skills or Institutions Shape Occupational Mobility?

#### Simulation results for now — awaiting linked census microdata

## Labour markets continually reallocate workers

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
- Demand for occupations shifts due to technological change, policy, and shocks
- Entry and exit absorb part of the adjustment, but some workers must move across occupations
- Some occupational transitions are harder than others
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/farside.jpg)
:::
:::::

## How does occupational distance shape mobility?

-   Workers tend to move between occupations with similar task requirements[@gathmann2010general]

$$
P_{ij} \downarrow \text{ as } C_{ij} \uparrow
$$

where $P_{ij}$ is the probability of moving from occupation $i$ to $j$, and $C_{ij}$ represents the mobility cost implied by occupational distance

- We therefore ask:

*Which notion of occupational distance best rationalizes local mobility?*

## What Defines Occupational Distance?

Two natural candidates:

**Skill similarity**: based on 161 O\*NET dimensions

**Institutional hierarchy**: based on 5 digit NOC taxonomy

## Comparing distance metrics

-   We model mobility using entropy-regularized optimal transport.

-   This allows competing distance matrices to be compared in a clean **horse race**

![.](images/horse.png){width="400px"}

## Two hypothesized mobility regimes

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
-   Local mobility: gradual movement in occupational space
-   Non-local mobility: jumps that bypass distance frictions, like a "wormhole" in occupation space.
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
![](images/worm.jpg)
:::
:::::

## Data partition

- We partition on whether highest educational attainment changed between 2016 and 2021

    - Unchanged: 2016 occupation is a meaningful origin — distance expected to rationalize observed mobility
    - Changed: new highest credential breaks the origin-destination link — distance should not rationalize mobility

- The changed-attainment partition serves as a negative control: a model fitting well there would undermine the structural interpretation of fit in the unchanged partition


## Local Mobility

-   Gravity-style mobility models predict that flows increase with origin and destination size and decline with distance

-   This mirrors the law of universal gravitation: $F \propto \frac{m_1 m_2}{d^2}$

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
- Objective: separate the mass effect (occupation size) from the distance effect in order to identify which distance measure best rationalizes local mobility
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/newton.jpeg)
:::
:::::

## Gravity models

- Commonly used to model migration, commuting, trade...

$$
P_{ij} = \exp(\alpha_i + \beta_j - \gamma C_{ij})
$$

-   $P_{ij}$ is the share of workers moving from occupation $i$ to $j$
-   $\alpha_i$ origin fixed effect
-   $\beta_j$ destination fixed effect
-   $C_{ij}$ proxy for the true mobility cost
-   $\gamma$ sensitivity of flows to proxy 

## Gravity Models: An Unfair Horse Race

- Gravity models jointly estimate cost sensitivity and fixed effects
- If the cost proxy $C_{ij}$ is misspecified — and it inevitably is — part of the misspecification is absorbed by the fixed effects

::::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}

- This allows a poorly specified cost matrix to appear to fit the data well
-  We prefer misspecification to appear as lack of fit rather than being masked by parameter adjustment

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

![](images/handi.png)
:::
:::::

## A Fair Horse Race

Entropy-regularized optimal transport imposes the observed origin and destination totals exactly

$$
\sum_j P_{ij} = a_i, \qquad
\sum_i P_{ij} = b_j
$$

- The model therefore cannot adjust fixed effects to compensate for cost misspecification

- Equilibrium employment levels are taken as given; we model mobility flows conditional on those levels.

- Equivalent to a multinomial logit random utility model with mobility costs and idiosyncratic Gumbel shocks.

## Our goal:

- cleanly identify how well each friction rationalizes the observed **flows**
- most workers remain in the same occupation over a five-year period
- even a crude switching-cost model (0 on the diagonal, +c elsewhere) will vastly outperform independence, which predicts flows as the outer product of the marginals
- our interest is explaining **where workers go when they move**, not simply **whether they move**

## Entropy-regularized optimal transport {.smaller}

$$
\mathcal{L}
=
\underbrace{\sum_{ij} P_{ij} C_{ij}}_{\text{mass}\times\text{distance}}
+
\varepsilon\times
\underbrace{\sum_{ij} P_{ij}(\log P_{ij}-1)}_{\text{negative entropy}}
+
\sum_i f_i \underbrace{\left(a_i - \sum_j P_{ij}\right)}_{\text{origin constraint}}
+
\sum_j g_j \underbrace{\left(b_j - \sum_i P_{ij}\right)}_{\text{destination constraint}}
$$

First-order conditions:

$$
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial P_{ij}}
=
C_{ij} + \varepsilon \log P_{ij} - f_i - g_j = 0
$$

Rearranging:

$$
\log P_{ij}
=
\frac{f_i}{\varepsilon}
+
\frac{g_j}{\varepsilon}
-
\frac{C_{ij}}{\varepsilon}
$$

## Structure of the Solution {.smaller}

Exponentiating:

$$
P_{ij}
=
u_i\, e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}\, v_j,
$$

-   Thus the optimal solution must be a row- and column-rescaling of the kernel $e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon}$
-   Given $v$, there is a unique $u$ that fixes the rows
-   Given $u$, there is a unique $v$ that fixes the columns
-   Sinkhorn alternates these corrections until both margins are satisfied
-   Implemented using a benchmark-tested log-domain Sinkhorn solver that ensures numerical stability and dimensional alignment

[![.](images/logo.png){width="400px"}](https://github.com/bcgov/safesink)

## Result

-   Because the objective is strictly convex, the optimal solution $P^{\star}$ is unique

-   If the Sinkhorn algorithm converges, it must converge to $P^{\star}$

The optimal solution:

-   matches the observed origin and destination totals
-   respects the relative friction structure implied by $C_{ij}$

## Same structure as gravity, but... {background-image="images/hammer.jpg" background-size="cover" background-opacity="0.5"}

Gravity estimates margins and frictions jointly

Sinkhorn conditions on the margins, so frictions are identified from the residual structure of flows

-   With a misspecified cost matrix, gravity simply estimates sensitivity to the wrong notion of distance

-   When the goal is to compare alternative cost matrices, conditioning on the margins allows cleaner identification of frictions

Sinkhorn is the right tool for this job

## Interpretation of Temperature: $\varepsilon$

-   $\varepsilon$ is the scale of Gumbel utility shocks affecting mobility choices

-   The temperature parameter governs how much mobility reflects cost minimization versus randomness

Low $\varepsilon$

-   Behavior approaches cost-minimizing reallocation (social planner)

High $\varepsilon$

-   Mobility becomes diffuse and approaches random choice $P_{ij} = a_i b_j$

## The distance metrics

-   Skill distance: represents continuous skill transferability
-   Hierarchical distance: represents discrete barriers within labour market

## Hierarchical distance: derived from NOC taxonomy {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="30%"}
1.  All five digits match:
    -   distance = 0\
2.  First four digits match:
    -   distance = 1\
3.  First three digits match:
    -   distance = 2\
4.  First digit matches:
    -   distance = 3 + \|ΔTEER\|\
5.  Otherwise:
    -   distance = 9\
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}

## Simulation Design

Generate artificial flows using

$$
C = (1-w)C_{skill} + wC_{hier}
$$

with

$$
\varepsilon = 1
$$

Then estimate models using:

-   $C_{skill}$
-   $C_{hier}$

## Evaluating the Horse Race

-   We evaluate model fit using the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the observed transition matrix $P$ and the predicted matrix $\hat P$

-   In our simulations $P$ is the true transition matrix, so KL measures the divergence between the estimated model and the truth

$$
KL(P \parallel \hat P)
=
\sum_{ij} P_{ij}\log\frac{P_{ij}}{\hat P_{ij}}
$$

-   KL divergence measures the **log-likelihood loss** of the model
-   **Lower values indicate better fit**

## Simulation: Can the method recover the true distance structure? {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="30%"}
- We evaluate fit over a range of temperatures as a robustness check: $\varepsilon \in  [0.5, 2], \varepsilon\neq1$.
- When the DGP matches the distance metric, that metric clearly dominates.
- When flows are independent, forcing distance to matter increases loss.
- When both structures are present, the race tightens.
:::

::: {.column width="70%"}
```{r}

 plots$kl_plots+
   theme(text=element_text(size=17.5), legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Is the labour market segmented?

-   Do different distance metrics explain mobility in different parts of the labour market?

-   One might hypothesize:

    -   hierarchical distance better rationalizes mobility into highly gated occupations

    -   skill distance better rationalizes mobility into less gated occupations

-   We split the data according to the concentration of educational pipelines into each occupation.

-   Education gating serves as a proxy for the tightness of occupational entry pathways.

## Destination education gating:

Some occupations draw from **very specific educational pipelines**, while others recruit from a broad mix of credentials

1.  Calculate overall workforce education distribution $p_0$
2.  Measure KL divergence of each occupation's education distribution $p$

$$
KL(p \parallel p_0)
$$

3.  Remove the mechanical relationship with occupation size $T$

$$
\text{specificity} = \log(KL) - \widehat{E}[\log(KL) \mid \log(T)]
$$

## Policy implication {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="35%"}
-   Labour shortages in different segments require different adjustment mechanisms

    -   High gating: adjustment depends on expanding formal training pipelines

    -   Low gating: reskilling and short-cycle training can accelerate adjustment

-   Shortages in highly gated occupations cannot be resolved quickly through reskilling alone
:::

::: {.column width="65%"}
```{r}
dest_plt <- dest_plt+
  theme(text=element_text(size=17.5))
p <- ggplotly(dest_plt, width=800,
  height=600)
p$x$data <- rev(p$x$data)
p
```
:::
:::::

## Heterogeneity in Distance Structure {.smaller}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="30%"}
-   To the right we see the result of splitting the labour market into destination gating quartiles
-   Treating the labour market as a whole would hide this structure
-   We could also split on the basis of destination TEER, as hierarchical distance may overstate cross-group frictions for TEERs 0 & 5
:::

## Individual analysis: the *attainment increase* group {.smaller}

-   Regress distance traveled on size-corrected KL divergence measures from the CIP–NOC table

    -   **Education specificity**\
        → How concentrated are graduates from a program across occupations\
        → Interpreted as likelihood the program acts as a **wormhole entrance**

    -   **Destination gating**\
        → How concentrated are entrants to an occupation across programs\
        → Interpreted as likelihood the occupation acts as a **wormhole exit**

-   Controls: 2-digit NOC origin fixed effects (2016 occupation)\
    → Origin occupation may influence both education choice and distance traveled

**Hypothesis**

-   More specific programs and more gated occupations should generate larger occupational jumps

## What we will do (once the linked data are available)

1)  Race two distance metrics on two samples:

    -   one where distance should rationalize local mobility (highest educational attainment constant)

    -   one where it should not (highest educational attainment changed)

2)  Test for heterogeneity in mobility frictions across the labour market:

    -   split sample by measure of destination gating and race the two metrics on each split

3)  Characterize the relationship between distance traveled and education/destination specificity among the *attainment increase* group
